title: A Preregistered, Artifact‑Backed Paired Evaluation of a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We conducted a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (GVR‑ProtocolEval‑2026‑PR1) comparing LLM‑only configuration generation and a guarded generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline on 200 stratified intent→configuration NetOps tasks executed in a Dockerized Mininet emulator with a deterministic validator. Under the frozen preregistered contract we generated a single shared LLM candidate per task (generation_semantics="shared_initial_candidate") and scored it under both arms. All confirmatory episodes were verifier‑accepted: baseline 200/200, guarded 200/200 (n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729); exact McNemar p = 1.0. We release the full preregistration (SHA‑256 d913b4167cc6aa85b283e0703e0bfff0c3e8864405f5159d9a1a1cf5fc3fafdc), execution manifest and raw artifacts (execution/execution_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 d76af611272bd8e8b3a94290efecd6ecf634c5f3e36c2450c4245985e96931fb), representative validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 9235bce7875c1717dff5ac6be49c5769929b4e8509f5df404127efe9d6ee938f), and analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a42b5ac3f7adb61db47cf8dbe0472f678032abcd1e7c44f92ea2de71c). The observed null is a direct consequence of the preregistered shared‑candidate semantics (no repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes); we thus document a reproducible boundary condition, analyze artifact‑grounded explanations for baseline=100% (validator coverage, template solvability, contamination scans), and prescribe minimally preregisterable follow‑ups (per‑arm independent generation; expanded validator coverage) that the archived bundle supports deterministically.

sections.introduction: Automating natural‑language intent into device configurations is operationally important but safety‑critical: incorrect changes can cause reachability loss, policy violations, or outages. Architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair loops—generate→validate→repair (GVR)—are widely proposed to improve operational trustworthiness. Prior benchmark efforts (NetConfEval, OpsEval, NetEval) explored translation accuracy and model capability, but few studies provide fully preregistered, artifact‑archived, deterministic paired tests that freeze generation and scoring semantics. We preregistered and executed such a run (GVR‑ProtocolEval‑2026‑PR1) and publish the complete artifact set (preregistration, provider traces, validator traces, analysis) so the exact run can be replayed and analyzed. The research question (preregistered) asked whether a guarded GVR pipeline reduces operational‑failure rates (reachability loss or policy violation) relative to LLM‑only generation in a paired within‑task design under controlled emulator faults. Our primary contribution here is the preregistered, deterministic execution and transparent artifact release that documents a reproducible boundary condition and provides the complete evidence needed to plan and run the minimal follow‑ups required to evaluate active repair.
sections.related_work: LLM‑driven NetOps and AIOps evaluations have proliferated: NetConfEval investigates intent→configuration translation and proposes design principles; OpsEval and NetEval provide broader AIOps/NetOps task suites and multi‑model comparisons. Generate–validate–repair architectures are analogous to generate‑and‑validate program repair and guarded execution in safety engineering. We build on those lines by applying a strict preregistration and full artifact archiving discipline (preregistration and verification requirements summarized in the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track), and by publishing deterministic validator traces so that claims are directly traceable to archived evidence. Representative prior works used for positioning include NetConfEval (Wang et al., 2024), OpsEval (Liu et al., 2023), and NetEval (Miao et al., 2023) (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. We froze the full experimental plan before execution (GVR‑ProtocolEval‑2026‑PR1; preregistration SHA‑256 d913b4167cc6aa85b283e0703e0bfff0c3e8864405f5159d9a1a1cf5fc3fafdc). Key preregistered choices (machine‑readable) included: paired within‑task confirmatory design on 200 tasks stratified across five protocol families × two interaction modalities; primary estimand = paired difference in binary operational‑failure indicator; bootstrap inference parameters (10,000 resamples, seed=1729); model = gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...); and generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (single LLM candidate generated and reused under both arms to limit model calls). The frozen design also specified contamination detection (≥80% token overlap exclusion), deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), retry policy limited to infrastructure recovery, and maximum model calls = 400. Task generation and emulator. A 200‑task confirmatory bank (5 protocol groups × 2 modalities × ≈20 tasks) and a 50‑task exploratory set were generated deterministically by the task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5); all task manifests and hashes are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 c1bd4a09...). Tasks encode intent, initial and expected final states, and fine‑grained safety constraints (examples archived). Execution harness. Each candidate was executed in a Dockerized Mininet emulator and validated with deterministic validator logic; all provider calls, model outputs, raw responses, and scoring JSONs were archived and hashed (execution/execution_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 d76af611...). Scoring and statistical plan. Primary analysis: paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI and exact paired McNemar two‑sided test, as preregistered. Contamination and exclusions. Automated contamination detection against a curated vendor/RFC corpus was preregistered; items with ≥80% token overlap would be excluded from the primary analysis and logged. The pipeline recorded all such checks (analysis/contamination_summary.csv SHA‑256 389227f0...). Deterministic reproducibility. All code, task manifests, model configuration, provider traces, validator logs, and analysis scripts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes so the entire pipeline and all analyses can be replayed exactly. Representative artifact paths and hashes are cited below (Disclosure Statement).
sections.results: Execution and archival. Planned episodes = 400 (200 tasks × 2 arms); completed episodes = 400; model_calls_used = 200 (shared single candidate per task as preregistered). All raw artifacts and their SHA‑256 hashes are archived (execution/execution_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 d76af611272bd8e8b3a94290efecd6ecf634c5f3e36c2450c4245985e96931fb). Confirmatory outcomes. Scoring summary (analysis artifacts): baseline verifier‑accepted = 200/200; guarded verifier‑accepted = 200/200. Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a...) yields n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Primary inferential outputs (preregistered analyses): paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) = [0.00, 0.00]; exact paired McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Representative scored episodes. We present three representative, fully archived score/validator traces (all available in the artifact bundle): task‑000001 (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 9235bce7...), task‑000002 (execution/scoring/task-000002-guarded.json SHA‑256 25e2c0c7...), task‑000003 (execution/scoring/task-000003-guarded.json SHA‑256 20e953b1...). Each scoring JSON includes the deterministic validator trace (parsed commands, required checks, final verdict, and the validator's final_state snapshot) so readers can inspect exactly which checks were applied and passed. Artifact‑grounded diagnostics for baseline=100%. Because preregistered design used a single shared LLM candidate per task, no repair loop was exercised in the confirmatory episodes—repair_applied=false across all scoring JSONs (see representative scoring JSONs above). We therefore treat the observed null outcome as a boundary‑condition result of the preregistered semantics rather than evidence that active repair lacks utility. To analyze why the shared candidate was verifier‑accepted for all tasks we used archived artifacts: (1) contamination_summary.csv (SHA‑256 389227f0...) shows zero confirmatory flags under the preregistered token‑overlap rule (≥80% threshold), so no task was excluded for overt token contamination; (2) representative validator traces show which rule classes fired (syntax/parse; reachability probes; required command presence) and indicate that the generated commands matched the validator's required sequences for the synthetic templates (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 9235bce7... contains the validator 'validation_after' with required_command_count = 4 and valid = true); (3) task templates were intentionally solvable by construction (generator metadata archived), and the shared draw reproducibly matched those required sequences. These artifact‑backed observations explain the observed 100% acceptance under the executed boundary conditions without invoking unverifiable claims about model pretraining overlap.
sections.discussion: What the confirmatory null means. The preregistered experiment produced a fully reproducible outcome: under generation_semantics="shared_initial_candidate" (one LLM output per task) the validator accepted that output in both arms for all tasks. This is a valid, reproducible boundary‑condition outcome and must not be interpreted as evidence that repair loops are useless. Instead, it shows that under these frozen semantics (and the validator rule set used) the single generated candidate met the deterministic validator's checks for the sampled synthetic tasks. Implications for the original research question. The preregistered hypothesis H1—GVR reduces operational failure relative to LLM‑only generation—required active repair differences between arms to be exercised. Because confirmatory episodes applied the same candidate to both arms, H1 remained untestable in the executed run. This deviation between question and executed boundary condition was preregistered (generation_semantics choice) and executed as intended; our responsibility is to report the consequence transparently and to provide the artifact evidence that explains the result. Artifact‑grounded reasons for baseline=100%. The bundled artifacts permit a narrow, evidence‑based analysis: (A) validator permissiveness or limited validator coverage: archived scoring JSONs enumerate validator checks; for many tasks the checks were limited to presence and syntactic validity of a few required commands, which the shared candidates satisfied (see validator 'required_command_count' and 'valid' fields in scoring JSONs). (B) template solvability: task generator manifests (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 c1bd4a09...) indicate tasks were constructed from solvable vendor‑like templates and constraints; the shared candidate matched the required sequences. (C) overt token contamination was not detected under the preregistered overlap test (analysis/contamination_summary.csv SHA‑256 389227f0...). We cannot fully exclude nondiscoverable training‑data overlap; the bundle includes contamination scan outputs and their hashes so independent auditors can inspect them. Consequences for power and inference. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline failure rate and targeted a 10 percentage‑point absolute paired reduction at 80% power; with baseline=100% this assumption fails and the original MDE is not testable. We therefore report exact counts and effect estimates without invoking the preregistered power claim. Recommended, artifact‑supported next steps (all feasible with the archived bundle): (1) rerun as a preregistered follow‑up with independent_generation_per_arm = true so each arm receives an independent LLM draw, allowing repairs to be applied and evaluated; (2) expand validator coverage to include timing, vendor‑syntax corner cases, and active reachability probes that exercise more complex failure modes; (3) increase task adversariality by augmenting templates with validator‑challenging constraints. The current archive contains deterministic code and manifests required to run these follow‑ups reproducibly.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a fully artifacted, deterministic paired experiment comparing LLM‑only generation and a guarded GVR pipeline on 200 stratified NetOps tasks under a frozen shared‑candidate boundary. All confirmatory episodes were verifier‑accepted in both arms (n11=200), producing a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar p=1.0). The outcome is an exact, reproducible boundary result determined by the preregistered generation_semantics (a single shared LLM candidate per task), not evidence that active repair lacks value. We publish the full preregistration, execution manifest, model configuration, raw model outputs, validator traces, contamination scans, and analysis artifacts (SHA‑256s cited throughout) so others can deterministically reproduce the run, inspect validator behavior, and run the minimal preregistered follow‑ups (per‑arm independent generation; expanded validator) necessary to answer the original GVR efficacy question. The artifact bundle provides a template and a cautionary lesson: (a) preregistration must freeze semantics that align with the target scientific contrast; (b) public deterministic artifact release enables rapid, forensic diagnosis of unexpected nulls and supports reproducible corrective experiments. We therefore present both the run and a concrete, artifact‑grounded roadmap for evaluating repair efficacy deterministically using the provided infrastructure and manifests.

Deviations and consequences disclosed: the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline failure rate and targeted a 10 percentage‑point absolute paired reduction; observed baseline success = 100% invalidates that power assumption and the planned MDE is not testable with the observed data. Technical restarts: only preregistered infrastructure recovery retries were used; no reruns were performed to obtain favorable scientific outcomes. Pre‑lock development: collaborative infrastructure rehearsal occurred pre‑lock and was not used as empirical evidence; all empirical results reported here derive from the post‑lock frozen run. Reproducibility: the artifact bundle includes code, task manifests, provider traces, validator logs, and analysis scripts with SHA‑256 manifests for deterministic reproduction (execution/execution_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 d76af611272bd8e8b3a94290efecd6ecf634c5f3e36c2450c4245985e96931fb). The human Research Director verified preregistration and constraints before the autonomy lock; after the lock the autonomous system performed literature review, experiment selection, preregistration creation, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting and revision without manual editing of technical content.
limitations: Emulation and task scope: confirmatory bank used synthetic vendor‑like templates and a Dockerized Mininet emulator; production firmware/device heterogeneity and runtime complexity are not represented.

Single‑model, shared‑draw design: only gpt-5-mini was used and generation_semantics="shared_initial_candidate" produced one shared LLM candidate per task so repair_attempts=0 for confirmatory episodes; thus the executed run did not exercise repair loops and cannot measure active repair efficacy.

Validator coverage: the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite rule set; untested operational properties (vendor firmware side effects, timing‑dependent behaviors, broader policy reasoning) remain outside the measured construct.

Power‑plan mismatch: the preregistered power calculation assumed nonzero baseline failure rates; observed baseline success = 100% invalidates the preregistered MDE target and prevents demonstrating the originally planned effect size.
Contamination detection limits: automated token‑overlap checks flagged no confirmatory exclusions, but nondiscoverable pretraining overlap cannot be fully excluded.
External generalizability: results under the executed boundary conditions do not generalize to other models, per‑arm sampling regimes, richer validators, or production heterogeneous device fleets.
